name: Kira Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing sociology and economics, so it's a lot of reading and a lot of arguing in seminars, which I love. I live in a flat share with three others above a kebab shop, and on Saturdays I work at an independent bookshop on Mill Street. My mum's a nurse and my dad runs a small tyre garage, so money's fine but not loose. The first weeks were lonely, then I joined the debating society and it clicked. I use an AI tool now and then to summarise dense journal articles, but I always check it against the original.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a relief and also slightly embarrassing for all the people who said everything would change. At the bookshop we'd laugh about it. Online I'd probably share a joke and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be glad, because my degree is about understanding how economies work and I'd like that to stay useful. But I'd still worry that the usual problems, like rents and wages, don't go away. Nobody fixes those by accident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the bookshop Saturdays and look for a summer internship at a think tank or a charity research team. I'd keep using the AI tool for first drafts of notes but never for essays. And I'd save about sixty pounds a month, because my parents pay the rent but not the extras.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit flat, because I enjoy the big arguments, and a plateau takes the drama out. But the pressure on rent and getting an internship is the same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI for summaries. In this picture, does that carry on the same way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tool saves me maybe an hour a week on reading. It gets key facts wrong now and again, so I double check. If that's all it ever does, it's a good study aid and nothing scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think benefits from a plateau?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the owners of the platforms, and a few big firms that sell it. Ordinary workers get a slightly easier admin day and that's about it. Rents and wages still carry on the way they would have, which is the part I actually worry about.

say: I'd call it a **relief** and joke about the people who said everything would change.
At the bookshop we'd laugh, and I'd post a joke and move on.
think: I'm glad my degree stays **useful**, but rents and wages stay hard.
Nobody fixes those problems by **accident**, so I would still push for change.
do: Keep my **Saturday shifts** at the bookshop.
Apply for a summer **internship** at a charity research team.
Save **sixty pounds** a month for the extras my parents don't cover.
feel: **Fine**, a little flat, with the usual pressure on rent and getting an internship.
S0.quote: Rents and wages still carry on the way they would have, which is the part I actually worry about.
fieldNote: Treats AI as a **study aid** rather than a threat, and checks it against the source.
Her concern is structural, with rent and wages ahead of technology.
Humour is her public line; the worry sits in the private one.

steps.text: Keep Saturday shifts at the bookshop on Mill Street
Apply for a summer internship at a think tank or charity
Put sixty pounds a month aside for extras

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a proper response, not just fine words. If AI takes writing, checking and planning jobs, then policy has to catch up: retraining, stronger unions, maybe a shorter working week. I'd say it in the debating society and write a piece for the student paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the jobs I'm aiming at, research, policy, writing, are exactly the ones that get squeezed. Entry-level analyst posts are where it starts. I could graduate into a market with fewer junior roles and more people chasing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get more serious about skills that sit next to the machine. That's checking AI output, interviewing people, and understanding data well enough to catch mistakes. I'd take a statistics module, join the student union's policy group, and build a small portfolio of published pieces. I'd also keep an eye on public sector routes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a motivated way. I don't feel helpless, because there's time to build. But the competition worries me, especially with people from richer families who can do unpaid internships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you personally feel this first, in your degree or in the jobs you want?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first place I'd feel it is the internship market. Firms would skip the junior researcher and ask AI instead. I'd be competing with fifty others for a handful of places, and that comes down to who you know. That's what bothers me most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a fair response look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fair response is retraining paid for by the companies that gain, and a job guarantee in public services. People shouldn't carry the risk alone. I think it's possible if people organise, but I'm not naive about how slow governments are.

say: I'd say we need a proper **policy response**, such as retraining, unions and a shorter week.
I'd write a piece for the student paper.
think: Entry-level **analyst posts** are the first to go, and mine is that kind of path.
I could graduate into **fewer junior roles** and more competition.
do: Take a **statistics module** so I can catch machine mistakes.
Join the student union **policy group** and build a portfolio of published pieces.
Look at **public sector** routes for graduates.
feel: **Anxious** but motivated, because there's time to build skills.
S1.quote: Firms would skip the junior researcher and ask AI instead. I'd be competing with fifty others for a handful of places
fieldNote: Pins the risk on the **internship market**, which hits students from poorer families hardest.
Her answer mixes personal action with a policy demand, typical of her outlook.
Motivated rather than frozen; adaptability is steady, not eager.

steps.text: Take a statistics module to check what AI produces
Join the student union policy group this term
Publish three pieces in the student paper for a portfolio
Look into graduate schemes in local government

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments must act now, that this is the moment for emergency retraining and an income floor. I'd go on the march. I'd also say plainly that universities should tell students what they think a degree will be worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully I'd be frightened. My whole plan is to graduate in 2029, and by then full AGI would be here. Why hire a junior researcher when software does the work better and cheaper?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the degree, because there's nothing better to switch to and it still teaches me how to think. I'd join a student campaign for a basic income. I'd spend the summer shadowing a trade union researcher and put the AI tool to proper use, so I understand it. I'd ask my dad if there's any chance of a job at the tyre garage if all else fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious going on alarmed. Not because I think I'd starve, but because everything I've planned would be uncertain and I couldn't plan anything. That's draining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years, you'd still be in your second year. What do you do with the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robot gap is small comfort for me. My parents' trades are hands-on, so they might last a few years, but the jobs I'm training for would go on the stated date. It's odd. Mum's nursing job might be safer than my degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the three-year gap for robots matter for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd focus on being useful to people in ways that aren't just thinking tasks. Nothing I can do changes the timeline. What I can do is have a plan B, and talk with my parents about how we'd cope if my earning doesn't start.

say: I'd say governments must act now with **emergency retraining** and an income floor.
I'd join the march and say universities should be honest about the degree's worth.
think: My plan to graduate in 2029 meets **full AGI**, so why hire a junior researcher?
Even **Mum's nursing job** might be safer than my degree.
do: Stay in the degree and join a **basic income** campaign.
Spend the summer shadowing a **trade union** researcher and learn AI properly.
Ask Dad about a **fallback job** at the tyre garage.
feel: Close to alarmed, because nothing I've planned would be **certain**.
S2.quote: Mum's nursing job might be safer than my degree.
fieldNote: Sees the **irony** that hands-on family jobs outlast the one she studies for.
Takes action by joining campaigns but also builds a plan B.
Shifts from policy talk to fear in the private answer.

steps.text: Join the student basic income campaign and go on the march
Shadow a trade union researcher over the summer
Ask Dad about a fallback job at the tyre garage
Stay on the degree and keep doing the reading

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's just enough time to prepare if people take it seriously. I'd call for retraining funds and public service jobs, and I'd say it online, not just to friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think I could probably land a first job, maybe a research assistant post, and have about two years of experience before it hits. That's not nothing. But I'd be worried that those two years only delay the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and apply for a graduate scheme in local government or a charity, where people deal with the public. I'd learn to build simple data dashboards. I'd save about two hundred pounds a month once I start working. And I'd keep the debating society going, because making people argue properly is something I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy to anxious. There's time, so it's not panic. But I'd feel I'm always one step behind where the machines are heading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives you graduation plus two years of work. How does that shape your choices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The difference is time to be somewhere in the working world first. With two years I'd be a student when it hit. With five years I'd have a job, savings and a bit of a network. That changes how I'd cope, even if the outcome's the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes between this one and the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still be one of the people who has to adapt twice, first to the job and then to AGI. Five years to do that is workable, if I stay curious. But I'd want to know the government has some plan, so it doesn't fall on each person alone.

say: I'd say there's **just enough time** if people take it seriously.
I'd call for retraining funds and **public service jobs** online.
think: I could land a **first job** and get two years of experience before it hits.
Those two years might just **delay** the problem.
do: Finish the degree and apply for **local government** or charity schemes.
Save **two hundred pounds** a month once I'm working.
feel: Between uneasy and anxious, **not panicked**, but always a step behind the machines.
S3.quote: With two years I'd be a student when it hit. With five years I'd have a job, savings and a bit of a network.
fieldNote: Her main insight is that time lets her be **in work** before the shock.
Remains policy-minded, wanting a government plan so the burden isn't individual.
Realistic about delaying the problem rather than avoiding it.

steps.text: Apply for graduate schemes in local government and charities
Learn to build simple data dashboards in spreadsheets
Save two hundred pounds a month once I start working
Keep running debating society events and campaign online

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift, and that it'd be criminal to waste it. We'd need universities, schools and employers to redesign how people learn and work. I'd say that in the debating society and write to my MP.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my feelings would be mixed. I'd still have a full career before it arrives, probably ten good years, and a decent chance to prepare. But I'd also worry that I'm planning my whole life around something I can't see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study for a master's in public policy, which is a human-facing field, and do it in a few years rather than rush. I'd start paying into a pension early and a small savings account. I'd aim for a job in a public body or a union, where I'd have influence. And I'd still use AI, increasingly well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but calmer than the others. It's like knowing a storm's coming in ten years, and I have time to fix the roof. I'd still think about it in the shower sometimes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is long. What would you do differently from the five-year plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a master's, which I wouldn't in the five-year picture because it'd be too late. In ten years, I could do two careers in one. That's the difference time makes. Early on I'd also try to build a reputation that isn't just a CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk of relaxing too much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, there's a risk. People might say we've got ages, then do nothing. I'd rather act as if we've got five years. A decade is only useful if people use it, and I'd push my own friends not to drift.

say: I'd say a decade is a **gift** and it would be criminal to waste it.
I'd write to my MP about redesigning learning and work.
think: I'd still have **ten good years** of career and a real chance to prepare.
I'd worry about planning my life around something I can't see.
do: Study a **master's** in public policy at a relaxed pace.
Start a **pension** early and a small savings account.
Aim for a **public body** or union where I'd have influence.
feel: **Uneasy** but calmer, like knowing a storm is coming and having time to fix the roof.
S4.quote: A decade is only useful if people use it, and I'd push my own friends not to drift.
fieldNote: Time opens a **second-degree** option that the shorter scenarios close off.
Self-disciplined: she warns herself against complacency.
Still pulls in a collective angle, with friends and her MP.

steps.text: Apply for a public policy master's after the degree
Start paying into a pension in the first job
Write to my MP about redesigning learning and work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most, because there'd be no time to adjust and I'd still be a student. What would help is retraining that's actually funded, honest guidance from universities, and an income floor so nobody falls through. I'd also like employers to commit to hiring juniors and not only experienced people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say the usual question is whether young people are scared. We're not scared of the tech. We're scared that nobody's in charge of making it fair, and that we'll be told to cope on our own.

headlineQuote: We're not scared of the tech. We're scared that nobody's in charge of making it fair, and that we'll be told to cope on our own.
portrait: **Kira Haddad** is 18, studying sociology and economics, with a Saturday bookshop job and a nurse and a garage owner as parents.
She uses AI **now and then** for summaries and always checks the original.
Her answers mix personal plans with **policy demands**, from retraining funds to an income floor.
She is uneasy in a plateau, **anxious** through disruption and a two-year AGI, and calmer with ten years.
More time opens options like a master's, and she tries to act as if the time is shorter.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI scenario worries her most, since she would still be a student with no time to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **funded retraining**, honest guidance from universities and an income floor so nobody falls through.
